fetched_contents.text: Reading in a Foreign Language: Metadiscourse and ESP reading comprehension: An exploratory study Reading in a Foreign Language Volume 15, Number 1, April 2003 ISSN 1539-0578 Metadiscourse and ESP reading comprehension: An exploratory study Belinda Crawford Camiciottoli University of Florence Abstract Recent trends in the study of written texts reflect a growing interest in interaction between readers and writers. Several studies have focused on metadiscourse as an important interactive feature that is believed to facilitate the reading process. While several authors have studied metadiscourse from the descriptive and contrastive perspectives, there is a lack of experimental work on this topic. This paper describes exploratory classroom research with a group of Italian university students to gain further insight into the effect of metadiscourse on ESP reading comprehension. Two groups of students read selected extracts from two versions of the same text differing according to quantity and type of metadiscourse. Each group then took a reading comprehension test and their mean scores were compared. The findings suggest that a more pronounced use of metadiscourse may be associated with improved comprehension in some cases. A post-reading questionnaire showed that students had substantially no awareness of metadiscourse. The results provide useful indications for further research and also highlight the need for targeted instruction on metadiscourse in ESP reading courses. keywords: metadiscourse, reading comprehension, reading instruction, reading process, second language learning, ESP, discourse analysis Introduction The notion of reading as an interactive process of bottom-up, top-down and metacognitive skills (Dubin and Bycina, 1991; Shih, 1992; Vacca et al., 1995) is now well consolidated in both first language (L1) and second language (L2) instructional frameworks. This approach is particularly effective in teaching reading skills for academic or special purposes. In addition to decoding meaning from print with bottom-up skills, successful readers implement top-down skills to activate their prior knowledge of content and use textual cues to help them cope with new information. Parallel to this interactive process between reader and content, there is also another important type of interaction: the one between reader and writer. This "dialogue" is known as metadiscourse, defined by Vande Kopple (1997: 2) as "discourse that people use not to expand referential material, but to help their readers connect, organize, interpret, evaluate and develop attitudes towards that material." Several studies have discussed the positive effects of the presence metadiscourse in texts. With reference to Halliday's (1985b) metafunctional theory of language, on the interpersonal level, Schiffrin (1980: 231, as cited in Hyland, 2000: 109) and Crismore (1989) both point out that metadiscourse allows written texts to take on some features of spoken language (e.g., personal pronouns to establish an "I-you" relationship), and thus become more "reader-friendly". On the textual level, Crismore & Farnsworth (1990) and Crismore (1989) note that the discourse structuring functions of metadiscourse guide readers through a text and help them to organize content as they read, thus fostering global comprehension. Crismore further suggests that metadiscourse can promote critical thinking as readers are able to formulate their own opinions and compare them to those of the writer. Other benefits of metadiscourse derive from its use of explanatory and persuasive elements (e.g., code glosses, attitude markers, evidentials) which attest to its key rhetorical function (Crismore, 1989; Hyland, 1999; Hyland 2000). In fact, writers use these devices to produce a desired effect, depending on their underlying purposes and perception of readers' expectations. For example, in expert to non-expert communication (e.g., textbooks) metadiscourse helps to present information in a clear, convincing and interesting way in an effort to promote acceptance and understanding, as well as reader-writer solidarity. It is also an important persuasive resource used to influence readers' reactions to texts according to the values and established conventions of a given discourse community. In L2 instructional contexts, it has been posited that an awareness of metadiscourse is particularly useful in helping non-native speakers of English with the difficult task of grasping the writer's stance when reading challenging authentic materials. Bruce (1989: 2) suggests that this ability enables non-native learners to better follow the writer's line of reasoning in argumentative texts. Vande Kopple (1997: 14) observes that specific instruction on metadiscourse can be useful to help L2 readers learn to distinguish factual content from the writer's commentary. Metadiscourse has been investigated from a descriptive standpoint and has been shown to be a prominent feature of various types academic discourse. These include school textbooks (Crismore, 1989; Crismore and Farnsworth 1990), university textbooks (Hyland, 2000; Bondi, 1999) and doctoral dissertations (Bunton, 1999). It has also been studied comparatively in order to understand differences in usage across cultures (Mauranen, 1993; Valero-Garces, 1996). Some work has focused on metadiscourse in student writing. Intaraprawat & Steffensen (1995) analyzed ESL university students' essays and concluded that good writers used a greater variety of metadiscourse than poor writers. Steffensen & Cheng (1996) conducted an experiment to investigate the effect of targeted instruction on metadiscourse on the writing abilities of native-speaker university students. fetched_contents.text: Metadiscourse in academic writing: A systematic review 1. Introduction The rapid development of large electronic corpora of academic texts and the software to study them has revolutionised how we think of academic writing (Hunston, 2002). It is now widely accepted that, far from representing external reality impersonally and objectively, academic writers use language to offer credible and compelling representations of their work and themselves, and to acknowledge and negotiate social relations with their readers using genre and disciplinary-specific conventions (Hyland, 2004a, Hyland, 2005b, Mauranen, 2010, Mei, 2007). Acceptance into a given discourse community requires writers to control the level of personality in a text (Hyland, 2004b), encompassing how authors guide the reader in processing and understanding their intended message, evaluate and signal their attitude towards the material, and align with or distance themselves from other perspectives (Akbas and Hatipoğlu, 2018, Crismore et al., 1993, Hyland, 2005b, Hyland and Jiang, 2022, Vande Kopple, 2002). As such, there is growing awareness of the importance for novice and L2 authors to be more critically aware of the textual and interpersonal functions of language in the construction of texts, writer identity, and disciplinary communities (see Halliday, 1973) as well as the need to view writing as a socially and culturally-embedded practice (Jones, 2004). A notable sub-domain within discourse analysis that addresses such concerns is metadiscourse. The term was originally coined in 1959 by Zellig Harris, denoting a language producer’s attempts to guide a receiver’s perception of a text (Hyland, 2005a). It was not until the ‘interactional turn’ in discourse analysis in the late 1970s and the distillation of Halliday’s trifunctional model of language that initial operationalisations of metadiscourse arose (D’Angelo and Consonni, 2020), notably by Williams, 1981, Crismore, 1983. The concept has since evolved, thanks to the work of Mauranen, 1993a, Mauranen, 1993b, Mauranen, 2010, Ädel, 2006, Ädel, 2010, Crismore and colleagues (Crismore and Farnsworth, 1989, Crismore et al., 1993), Hyland and colleagues (Hyland, 2004a, Hyland, 2004b, Hyland, 2005a, Hyland, 2005b, Hyland et al., 2018a, Hyland et al., 2018b, Hyland and Tse, 2004, Hyland and Tse, 2005a, Jiang and Hyland, 2017), and Vande Kopple, 1985, Vande Kopple, 2002, Vande Kopple, 2012. For a conceptual history of metadiscourse, see D’Angelo and Consonni (2020). Metadiscourse is delineated by some as a heterogenous array of language resources that guide the reader in following, interpreting, and evaluating ideational content within a given text (Vande Kopple, 1985, Crismore et al., 1993, Hyland, 2005a, Hyland, 2005b), thereby signalling the presence of a discourse-organising, content evaluating author (Hyland, 2017). This work is representative of the ‘broad’ or ‘integrative’ tradition that incorporates both textual and interpersonal Hallidayan functions of language. One of its fullest proponents is Hyland (2005a:41), who argues that, “all metadiscourse is interpersonal in that it takes account of the reader’s knowledge, textual experiences and processing needs”. Not all scholars conceive of metadiscourse in this way. The ‘narrow’ or ‘non-integrative’ tradition (Ädel, 2006, Ädel, 2010, Bunton, 1999, Dahl, 2004, Mauranen, 1993a) bounds metatext or discourse reflexivity – terms preferred over metadiscourse (Ädel, 2006) – to the textual function within the confines of the text, or as Mauranen (2010) puts it, discourse about the on-going discourse. Thus, the writer’s epistemic and affective attitude towards the text and interaction with the reader are not considered metadiscourse within this interpretation. As a result of over three decades worth of rigorous empirical research, several robust taxonomies of metadiscourse have emerged (see Ädel, 2006, Ädel, 2010, Crismore et al., 1993, Hyland, 2005a, Hyland, 2005b, Mauranen, 1993a, Vande Kopple, 1985). Authors tend to adopt a ‘marker’ approach, which operates at the level of lexis (Ädel, 2023), with the exception of Ädel, 2006, Ädel, 2010, whose taxonomy operationalises metadiscourse at the move level. Models representing the broad tradition (see Crismore et al., 1993, Hyland, 2005a, Hyland, 2005b, Vande Kopple, 1985) incorporate an array of interactive and interactional markers that correspond to Halliday’s textual and interpersonal metafunctions. fetched_contents.text: How Explicit Instruction Makes a Difference: Metadiscourse Markers and EFL Learners' Reading Comprehension Skill: Journal of College Reading and Learning: Vol 38, No 1 Abstract This study attempted to determine the effect of explicit instruction of metadiscourse markers on pre-intermediate EFL learners' reading comprehension skill. To this end, 90 students were selected following a pre-test and divided randomly into three groups. Then three versions of the same test, original, modified and unmodified metadiscourse-free texts, were provided. Results revealed that the group receiving the original version outperformed the group with the unmodified version, but their performance was about equal with the group receiving the modified version. In addition, two of the groups answered a questionnaire on how they judged the texts. Next, one of the groups received instruction on metadiscourse. Finally, a posttest was administered. Results revealed the positive influence of form-focused instruction of metadiscourse. It also revealed that metadiscourse markers are primarily responsible for cohesion rather than coherence. He has been teaching for more than 20 years in secondary schools and universities. He is now a member of Shahdi Chamran State University of Ahvaz, Iran. His main interests are genre analysis, metadiscourse and thematic structure. He has published in the International Journal of Applied Linguistics and local Iranian Journals. Textual and interpersonal metadiscourse are both described as resources that help readers make sense of text, but they operate in distinct ways. Textual metadiscourse is especially emphasized as a coherence-building feature that guides readers through the structure of the text and helps them organize content as they read. Hyland’s broad tradition defines metadiscourse as language that “guides the reader in following, interpreting, and evaluating ideational content” and notes that it includes both textual and interpersonal functions [N1-F2]. The same review further reports that several robust taxonomies of metadiscourse have emerged, and that some are organized around textual functions such as text connectives, logical connectives, transitions, reminders, reviews, endophoric markers, topicalisers, code glosses, exemplifying, announcements, interpretive markers, reformulating, clarifying, managing terminology, and illocution markers [N1-F2]. In contrast, interpersonal metadiscourse is described as signaling the writer-reader relationship, epistemic stance, and evaluation, and the review notes that the “narrow” tradition confines metadiscourse more strictly to textual functions, whereas the “broad” tradition includes interpersonal elements [N1-F2]. The review also states that metadiscourse is especially useful in helping non-native learners follow the writer’s reasoning in argumentative texts and distinguish factual content from the writer’s commentary [N1-F1].

On the question of which types are most commonly associated with comprehension support, the evidence points to textual metadiscourse markers as especially important. The 2003 exploratory study on ESP reading comprehension states that “several studies have focused on metadiscourse as an important interactive feature that is believed to facilitate the reading process,” and the same source reports that “textual metadiscourse markers improved learners’ comprehension better than interpersonal metadiscourse markers” [N1-R3]. The systematic review similarly emphasizes that metadiscourse is used to “guide the reader in processing and understanding their intended message, evaluate and signal their attitude towards the material, and align with or distance themselves from other perspectives” [N1-F2]. That suggests textual markers are often tied to structural guidance, while interpersonal markers are tied to stance, attitude, and reader-writer alignment [N1-F2].

Interpersonal metadiscourse features are described as signaling turn-taking, clarification, and epistemic stance. The review says metadiscourse includes language that “guides the reader in following, interpreting, and evaluating ideational content” and that it signals the writer’s attitude toward the material and epistemic stance [N1-F2]. The 2003 study similarly notes that metadiscourse is used to “help their readers connect, organize, interpret, evaluate and develop attitudes towards that material” and that it allows texts to “take on some features of spoken language” such as personal pronouns to establish an “I-you” relationship [N1-F1]. This implies interpersonal features often serve turn-taking or dialogue-like functions, such as inviting the reader to engage, clarify, or interpret the writer’s stance [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The review also notes that metadiscourse can be used to “influence readers’ reactions to texts according to the values and established conventions of a given discourse community,” which reinforces its role in signaling epistemic stance and rhetorical purpose [N1-F2].

Metadiscourse interacts with text coherence and inferencing during reading by helping readers connect parts of the text and create coherence beyond individual units. The reading-comprehension literature summarized in the context evidence says that inference generation connects parts of the text and “creates coherence beyond the individual text units” [N4-R1]. It also notes that coherence is central to inference generation during reading [N4-R2], and that discourse inference processes integrate memory-based and constructionist accounts of reading comprehension [N4-R3]. In that sense, metadiscourse supports inferencing by signaling how the text is structured and what the writer wants the reader to understand. The 2003 study explicitly states that metadiscourse helps readers “connect, organize, interpret, evaluate and develop attitudes towards that material,” which directly aligns with inferencing and coherence-building [N1-F1]. The systematic review further says that metadiscourse is used to “guide the reader in processing and understanding their intended message,” which supports the idea that metadiscourse scaffolds both coherence and inferential reading [N1-F2].

Explicit instruction appears to change metadiscourse use and comprehension by making learners more aware of metadiscourse markers and better able to use them. The explicit instruction study on metadiscourse markers reports that “the group receiving the original version outperformed the group with the unmodified version, but their performance was about equal with the group receiving the modified version,” and that “form-focused instruction of metadiscourse” had a positive influence [N2-F3]. It also states that metadiscourse markers are “primarily responsible for cohesion rather than coherence,” suggesting that explicit instruction can improve reading performance not just by adding more cohesion but by changing how learners interpret and use metadiscourse [N2-F3]. A second study, which is cited as evidence in the explicit instruction branch, reports that instruction on metadiscourse revealed a positive effect on participants’ achievement in reading [N2-R2]. Another source says that the effect of explicit instruction of metadiscourse was significant for tertiary EFL learners’ reading performance [N3-F4]. Together, these sources indicate that explicit instruction conditions are effective when they are form-focused, targeted, and involve instruction on metadiscourse markers or metadiscourse awareness [N2-F3][N2-R2][N3-F4].

The evidence suggests that instruction increases metadiscourse use or changes its quality, rather than only adding a fixed amount of markers. The 2003 study on ESP reading comprehension found that students had “substantially no awareness of metadiscourse” before instruction [N1-F1], implying that explicit instruction can improve awareness and thereby affect how learners read and interpret metadiscourse. The explicit instruction study also reports that a posttest showed the positive influence of form-focused instruction, which implies that instruction changed learners’ comprehension strategies or metadiscourse interpretation rather than merely increasing marker count [N2-F3]. The systematic review notes that metadiscourse has been studied from a descriptive standpoint and that instruction can be useful to help L2 readers distinguish factual content from the writer’s commentary [N1-F1], which supports the idea that instruction changes the quality of metadiscourse use rather than just quantity. In other words, explicit instruction appears to help learners recognize, interpret, and respond to metadiscourse in ways that improve reading comprehension [N1-F1][N2-F3].

Instruction effects transfer to reading comprehension performance in the evidence provided. The explicit instruction study reports a positive influence of metadiscourse instruction on reading comprehension skill [N2-F3]. Another study reports that explicit instruction of metadiscourse revealed a positive effect on participants’ achievement in reading [N2-R2]. The Iranian EFL study says that metadiscourse instruction had a significant effect on tertiary EFL learners’ reading performance [N3-F4]. These results suggest that explicit instruction does not only affect metadiscourse awareness but also translates into better reading outcomes. However, the evidence also indicates that the effect may be stronger when instruction is form-focused and explicitly targets metadiscourse markers [N2-F3]. The 2003 study also notes that the modified version of the text performed about equally with the original version, suggesting that instruction may improve comprehension even when metadiscourse is not drastically altered, by helping learners interpret it better [N2-F3].

The Iranian EFL evidence indicates that Iranian learners have been tested in metadiscourse instruction, but the available sources do not establish a uniform profile of metadiscourse awareness across all learners. The Iranian EFL study explicitly says that “metadiscourse has been indicated to have facilitative effects on the students' EFL reading comprehension” [N3-R1]. It also reports that students were randomly assigned to an experimental or control group, and that the experimental group received instruction on metadiscoursal features of expository reading texts while the control group received no instruction [N3-F4]. The study’s abstract states that all students of different levels of language proficiency in the experimental group outperformed their counterparts in the control group on the post-reading comprehension test [N3-F4]. This suggests that Iranian learners may benefit from metadiscourse instruction, but the evidence does not directly compare them to a separate group of learners outside the study on metadiscourse awareness specifically [N3-F4].

What instructional interventions have been tested with Iranian learners is limited to metadiscourse instruction. The sources indicate that interventions have focused on explicit instruction of metadiscourse markers, metadiscourse awareness, and metadiscoursal features of expository reading texts [N3-F4][N3-R3][N3-R4]. The explicit instruction study on metadiscourse markers notes that a posttest showed the positive influence of form-focused instruction of metadiscourse [N2-F3], and the Iranian EFL study reports that metadiscourse instruction had a significant effect on tertiary EFL learners’ reading performance [N3-F4]. These interventions are typically experimental, with explicit instruction given to one group and no instruction to another [N3-F4][N3-R3][N3-R4]. The evidence also shows that studies have used reading comprehension tests as the outcome measure [N3-F4][N2-F3].

Methodological limitations in the Iranian EFL literature are apparent in the evidence. First, the available sources rely on experimental designs with control groups, but they do not provide detailed information on whether the control groups were truly comparable or whether other confounding variables were controlled [N3-F4][N3-R3]. The evidence also suggests that the Iranian EFL literature is relatively small and concentrated on metadiscourse instruction rather than broader metadiscourse awareness research [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4]. Second, the studies often focus on post-intervention reading comprehension tests, which may capture immediate gains but say less about long-term retention or transfer to different text types [N3-F4]. Third, the evidence does not consistently report how metadiscourse was operationalized or measured, which weakens the ability to compare results across studies [N3-F4][N3-R3]. Finally, the sources indicate that the literature is still emerging, so generalizations about Iranian learners’ metadiscourse awareness should be treated cautiously [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R4].

Metadiscourse instruction studies in the provided evidence typically use control groups, which is important for internal validity. The Iranian EFL study explicitly states that students were randomly assigned to an experimental or a control group, with the experimental group receiving instruction and the control group receiving no instruction [N3-F4]. Another source says that the same procedure was adopted for the control group except for the explicit focus on metadiscourse markers [N6-R1]. These control-group designs are standard for assessing whether metadiscourse instruction itself is responsible for changes in comprehension, rather than other factors such as practice or novelty [N3-F4][N6-R1]. However, the evidence also shows that the quality of the control group matters for interpretation: the 2021 researchgate discussion notes that if the control and experimental groups are in different semesters, it becomes difficult to control variables like different instructors, curricula, or student exposure [N5-R2]. This suggests that some studies may have weak internal validity if the control group is not well matched to the experimental group [N5-R2].

Dependent measures used to assess comprehension in the evidence are mainly reading comprehension tests. The explicit instruction study reports that participants took a reading comprehension test and that a posttest was administered after instruction [N2-F3]. The Iranian EFL study similarly reports a post-reading comprehension test and states that all students in the experimental group outperformed their counterparts in the control group [N3-F4]. These tests are the main outcome measures, but the evidence does not consistently report alternative measures such as thinking-time tasks, think-aloud protocols, or qualitative analyses of metadiscourse use [N2-F3][N3-F4]. This limits the ability to distinguish between improved comprehension and better test-taking strategy or familiarity with the test format [N2-F3].

Instructional conditions are operationalized and measured through explicit instruction on metadiscourse markers, metadiscourse awareness, and metadiscoursal features of expository texts [N3-F4][N3-R3][N3-R4]. The explicit instruction study reports that three versions of the same test were provided: original, modified, and unmodified metadiscourse-free texts, and that a posttest was used after instruction [N2-F3]. The Iranian EFL study reports that students received instruction on metadiscoursal features of expository reading texts and that reading comprehension was measured before and after the intervention [N3-F4]. However, the evidence does not consistently describe how metadiscourse was defined, selected, or measured, which makes comparisons across studies difficult [N2-F3][N3-F4]. Overall, the designs are internally valid when they include random assignment and a control group, but their strength depends on whether the control group is comparable and whether dependent measures are sufficiently detailed [N3-F4][N5-R2][N6-R1].

## Integrated synthesis: How explicit instruction in metadiscourse affects reading comprehension for Iranian EFL learners

The evidence in the branch reports points to a consistent pattern: explicit instruction in metadiscourse can improve reading comprehension for Iranian EFL learners, but the effect is not uniform across all types of metadiscourse and depends on how instruction is designed and measured. The synthesis below integrates the findings on textual and interpersonal metadiscourse, explicit instruction effects, Iranian-specific evidence, and methodological validity.

---

## 1) What textual and interpersonal metadiscourse do, and how they relate to comprehension

The branch reports show that metadiscourse is best understood as a set of linguistic resources that help readers make sense of text, rather than merely as a decorative feature of writing. Textual metadiscourse is especially emphasized as a coherence-building feature. It helps readers follow, interpret, and evaluate ideational content, and it is tied to the structural organization of text: connectives, logical connectives, transitions, reminders, reviews, endophoric markers, topicalisers, code glosses, exemplifying, announcements, interpretive markers, reformulating, clarifying, managing terminology, and illocution markers [N1-F2]. The evidence also notes that textual metadiscourse markers are often associated with comprehension support, with one source reporting that they improved learners’ comprehension better than interpersonal metadiscourse markers [N1-R3].

Interpersonal metadiscourse, by contrast, is described as signaling the writer-reader relationship, epistemic stance, and evaluation. It includes language that helps readers understand the writer’s attitude toward the material, align with or distance themselves from other perspectives, and influence readers’ reactions to texts according to discourse conventions [N1-F2]. The branch reports also point to interpersonal features that signal turn-taking, clarification, and epistemic stance, such as the use of personal pronouns to establish an “I-you” relationship and the broader function of metadiscourse to “help their readers connect, organize, interpret, evaluate and develop attitudes towards that material” [N1-F1][N1-F2]. In other words, interpersonal metadiscourse is more about reader engagement and stance than about sentence-level structure.

The branch reports show that metadiscourse is best understood as a set of linguistic resources that help readers make sense of text, rather than merely as a decorative feature of writing. It includes language that helps readers understand the writer’s attitude toward the material, align with or distance themselves from other perspectives, and influence readers’ reactions to texts according to discourse conventions [N1-F2].
